St. Charles Borromeo speaks as if this practice of praying for forty hours was very ancient; he refers it to the forty hours that Christ's Body remained in the tomb . The number 40 is also associated with the rain at the time of the Flood , years the Israelites spent on the way to the Promised Land, and Jesus fasting for 40 days before beginning his public ministry.[ The 40 Hours Devotion is an experience cantered on inviting people to "face-to-face" time with Jesus, present in the Blessed Sacrament. It is a worthy devotion, one that helps the faithful encounter the Risen Lord in a personal way, nurturing their relationship with him. As St. Alphonsus Liguori once wrote: “Of all devotions, that of adoring Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament is the greatest after the sacraments, the one dearest to God and the one most helpful to us” . Pope Leo has asked us to ‘pray the rosary for peace with the particular intention that wars may cease and that peace may be established among peoples in conflict .” He also said: “Let us accompany this prayer with concrete acts of penance and mercy, committing ourselves always to fostering dialogue and reconciliation ”. THE RELICS OF THE VENERABLE MATT TALB OT 19th–22nd November 2026 will visit ‘ Star of the Sea’ Partnership, for a 4 day programme of prayer, reflection and other events. Matt Talbot is a much-loved figure in Dublin and throughout the world. His remarkable journey from addiction to a life of deep prayer and faith continues to inspire countless people. His story offers hope and encouragement to those facing difficulties and searching for peace, strength and the help that only God can give. Book Review: "Loss: The New Collection" by Donna Ashworth Grief is a landscape that every one of us will have to walk through at some point in our lives.
It is the price we pay for love, yet when it arrives, it can feel incredibly isolating, confusing, and overwhelming.

For anyone currently n avigating the dark valleys of bereavement, or for those seeking the right words to comfort a friend, Donna Ashworth’s newly expan ded book, Loss: The New Collection, offers a gentle sanctuary.
Ashworth, a bestselling poet known for her deep emp athy and emotional clarity, has compiled a beautifu l Treasury of words explicitly designed to meet people in their quietes t, heaviest moments.
Rather than offering clinical advice or hollow platitudes, the book presents short, accessible poems and refle ctions that act like a warm hand to hold during the darkest days of sorrow.
One of the most profound reminders woven throughout this collection is that grief is not a problem to be solved or an illness to be cured.
Instead, Ashworth gently reveals that gre at grief is simply the continuation of great love.

She honours the unpredictability of mourning—how it comes in waves, shifting from total numbness to sharp heartbreak—a nd reassures the reader that every feeling is a normal part of the h ealing process.
For our parish community, this book serves as an in valuable resource.
It is a thoughtful gift for some one who has recently lost a spouse, parent, child, or dear friend.
Because the pieces are short and bite-sized, it is perfect for a grieving heart that may find it difficult to concentrate on a heavy, lengthy book.
Loss: The New Collection , reminds us that while losing someone casts us adrift, we do not walk the pat h to healing alone.
It is a comforting, hopeful addition to any bedside table a nd a reminder of the enduring power of love.
